newsitem.title: UK: IRA trying to wreck peace hopes - Loyalist leader.
newsitem.headline: IRA trying to wreck peace hopes - Loyalist leader.

text.p: A pro-British Loyalist leader accused his republican foes on Thursday of trying to wreck Northern Ireland's struggling peace efforts after a huge IRA guerrilla bomb was discovered in Belfast.

"This is yet another indication that IRA (Irish Republican Army) is not genuinely interested in building a meaningful peace process," Gary McMichael said after security forces found some 1,000 pounds (450 kg) of explosives in an abandoned van.

The haul, the latest in a series of guerrilla incidents heightening tension in the British province, deepened gloom over attempts to end decades of conflict and triggered fears of retaliatory violence by rival guerrillas.

"The quantity of the explosives suggests that they were intending to explode a massive bomb and their objective was to cause optimum injury or loss of life. This does not bode well for the possibility of an inclusive peace process," said McMichael, who leads the Ulster Democratic Party.

"Loyalists are fast coming to the conclusion that we are being driven towards conflict by the IRA....We (UDP) will be doing everthing in our power to ensure that the (Loyalist) ceasefire remains intact," McMichael, whose party is the political arm of banned Loyalist extremists, told Reuters.

Anxiety that the region could slide into a cycle of tit-for- tat violence has been fuelled by two recent booby-trap attacks on senior republicans which media reports have blamed on Loyalists out to avenge IRA hostilities.
Commanders of the Loyalist extremists, so-called because of an unswerving allegiance to the British rule, have remained silent about the attacks.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew on Wednesday condemned the attacks but said he did not think that a Loyalist two-year truce had ended.
Mayhew described the IRA as "criminal gangsters" for leaving the van-bomb in the grounds of Belfast Castle, a 19th century mansion now used as a restaurant and conference centre.
Maintenance of the Loyalist truce is seen crucial to the province's peace hopes and for progress in fractious multi-party talks that opened last June.
Mayhew warned that any influence the Loyalist guerrillas' political wings had at the talks would be squandered if pro- British guerrillas ditched their ceasefire.
The IRA telephoned a warning to media organisations on Tuesday saying they had abandoned a landmine in the van, after spotting high-level British security activity in the area.
Police stepped up security and urged vigilance by the public as the van contents, which including detonating cord and bomb components, were made safe.

"We have been warning for some time of the likelihood of terrorist atacks and have taken steps to counter efforts of paramilitary groups to inflict further death and destruction," said William Davidson, deputy police commander for Belfast.
Earlier John Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party which speaks for most of the Catholic nationalist minority, made a fresh plea to the IRA to lay aside its weapons.

"I believe we must still work to deliver what the mass of our people want. This is a strong message to the IRA and to any of other paramilitary organisation, that the mass of our people want peace on our streets...My New Year message to the IRA is to respect that wish," he told BBC radio.
Britain insists the IRA, fighting to end British rule, must call a ceasefire to win a seat for its Sinn Fein political wing in talks. Sinn Fein wants an unconditional place at the talks.
